title: Companies That Helped Gut EU Climate Law Turn Up for COP31
author: Nancy Skinner

The Trump administration decided for the second year running to ignore the
annual UN climate talks, which opened last week in Antalya, Turkey. But the
companies behind one of the most successful recent corporate campaigns against
climate rules showed up in force, and their PR company is handling
communications for host country Turkey.

At least 41 people from seven companies that participated in a secretive and
ultimately successful lobbying campaign to roll back a key European climate
law are registered for COP31, according to a UN list of participants reviewed
by Drop Site. Most of them are not registered under their companies' names.

Back in 2024, the European Union passed a climate law--called the Corporate
Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)--requiring its biggest
companies, including American corporations doing business there, to do three
things: adopt and follow a plan to cut emissions in line with the Paris
Agreement's goal of holding the global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees
Celsius, clean up human rights and environmental abuses in their supply
chains, and answer to victims of such abuses in an EU-wide court.

In response, an alliance of 11 multinational corporations formed a group
calling itself the "Competitiveness Roundtable." Its members included Chevron,
ExxonMobil, Koch, TotalEnergies, Honeywell, Baker Hughes, Dow, Nyrstar,
Enterprise Mobility and JPMorgan Chase, the largest financier of fossil fuels.
Between March and August 2025, the group held 17 coordination meetings,
according to leaked [documents published](https://www.somo.nl/the-secretive-
cabal-of-us-polluters-that-is-rewriting-the-eus-human-rights-and-climate-law/)
by the Dutch research group SOMO. Teneo, a New York-based PR and advisory
firm, coordinated it.

By 2026, their mission had been accomplished and the CSDDD had been gutted.

The 41 people from Competitiveness Roundtable companies registered at COP31
are not the only industry representives at the conference. More than 100
companies and groups linked to fossil fuels were [identified last week
](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/13/cop31-companies-and-
groups-linked-to-fossil-fuels-
delegations?utm_term=6afc42efaa278056d854a974304b699d)by the [Kick Big
Polluters Out coalition](https://kickbigpollutersout.org/). Teneo, the
Competitiveness Roundtable's publicist, currently has a $3.9 million contract
to handle communications for COP31's host, the government of Turkey.

Drop Site asked the seven companies--ExxonMobile, Dow, Baker Hughes,
Honeywell, JPMorganChase, Total Energy, and Chevron--and Teneo about their
participation in the Competitiveness Roundtable. None of them provided
comments.

## **" Divide and Conquer"**

The Roundtable's strategy was explicit. It planned to "[divide and conquer in
the Council](https://www.somo.nl/the-secretive-cabal-of-us-polluters-that-is-
rewriting-the-eus-human-rights-and-climate-law/)," the body of EU governments,
by assigning member companies to work specific capitals. It aimed to sideline
"stubborn" EU departments and to push the center-right European People's Party
to side with the far right "as much as possible." SOMO found at least three
meetings in the documents that do not appear in the EU's lobbying transparency
register at all, and eight more that listed only Teneo, not the Roundtable
lobbying participants, at plenary sessions in Strasbourg.

And it foregrounded Trump's tariffs on EU goods. The Roundtable discussed
using European carmakers' desperation for tariff relief to get the CSDDD
scrapped or diluted "as a concession in negotiations on tariffs," according to
the SOMO documents. Chevron and ExxonMobil were assigned to build pressure
from outside Europe by pushing climate laws up the agenda of the U.S.-EU trade
talks.

Many of the companies never said a word against the law in public. Instead,
they lobbied the member states behind the scenes and largely kept their
opposition quiet. ExxonMobil did speak out. Chairman and CEO Darren Woods,
attending COP31 under the badge of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, [told
Bloomberg](https://worldoil.com/news/2025/9/18/exxon-ceo-slams-eu-climate-and-
human-rights-directive-as-threat-to-oil-and-gas-competitiveness) in 2025 it
was "the worst piece of legislation I've seen since I've been in this job,"
and [said](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/exxon-seeks-us-political-
help-111017284.html) its penalties would be "bone-crushing." In another
interview, Woods [said](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/exxon-seeks-us-
political-help-111017284.html) he had spoken directly with Trump about the
European law. That year, in response to criticism from companies in France and
Germany, the European Commission proposed a set of changes to weaken the
regulations.

Within six months, the deal was done. On July 27, 2025, at Trump's Turnberry
golf resort in Scotland, he and European Commission President Ursula von der
Leyen agreed to a 15% ceiling on most EU goods, including cars.

The fine print came on August 21, in a [joint
statement](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/08/joint-
statement-on-a-united-states-european-union-framework-on-an-agreement-on-
reciprocal-fair-and-balanced-trade/) published by the White House in which the
EU committed to "to address U.S. concerns" about the CSDDD's reach over non-EU
companies.

In short, the EU agreed to water down the climate law's emissions requirements
and the rules focused on human rights abuses. The deal became law in February
2026. The climate plan requirement was deleted outright. The EU-wide right to
sue was scrapped, leaving victims to each country's courts. The law now covers
only companies with more than 5,000 employees and €1.5 billion in total sales,
and not until July 2029.

post-

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e4214e9-a56e-434d-9c6d-306dac270789_2048x1463.png)

The EU's position was that the deal reflected its own "simplification" agenda,
first proposed in February 2025, before Turnberry. And that is true. The
Competitiveness Roundtable had already laid the groundwork on both sides of
the Atlantic. The trade deal turned a contested domestic proposal into a
written commitment to Washington.

The payoff did not buy economic peace. In May 2026, Trump announced he would
raise tariffs on European cars to 25%, accusing Brussels of moving too slowly.
The EU completed ratification of the Turnberry deal on June 25. By then, the
climate rules were already gone.

None of this proves the companies are in Antalya to lobby on any particular
decision. They are doing what large companies do at every COP: meeting
ministers, speaking on panels, selling technology.

Democrats sent a large delegation to COP31, led by California Gov. Gavin
Newsom, that's trying hard to rehabilitate the United States' climate
reputation, but they don't have a seat at the negotiating table.

The talks run until November 20. The central fight in the final-draft
negotiations is over whether it will include language on "transitioning away"
from fossil fuels or "phasing out" fossil fuels. But looming over the whole
enterprise is September's warning from the UN Environment Program that global
warming will now overshoot the Paris goal of 1.5°C within a few years, with
even the best case scenario peaking at 1.7 to 1.8°C. "There are no good
outcomes above 1.5 degrees C," the agency warned.

The country that has historically emitted more carbon than any other--the
United States--has withdrawn its pledges and its negotiators. The companies
whose coalition helped delete Europe's climate-plan requirement--call them the
"Overshoot Lobby"--have registered dozens of staff at this year's talks, many
as guests of the host. And the PR firm that coordinated that climate rollback
has been hired to tell the world what the summit achieved and what work
remains to be done.

Climatologist Michael Mann, professor of earth and environmental science at
the University of Pennsylvania and author of "Science Under Siege," told Drop
Site that laws "with teeth like the EU's CSDDD were moving in the right
direction." But now we have "oil-soaked PR firms like Teneo running
interference," he said.

"The fossil fuel lobby has filled the vacuum left behind by the U.S.
government at COP31," Mann added. "Decarbonization is a NOW issue, not a
transition issue, which is where the final draft is stuck."
